issues.title: quick & incomplete review of the editor’s copy
issues.author: thomas-fossati
issues.body:
### General comments

We should either s/transport/secure transport/g (or secure channel) or establish the equivalence of the terms (within the scope of this document) very early on.

We could add Gene Spafford’s usual quote somewhere: "Cryptography [without system integrity] is like investing in an armored car to carry money between a customer living in a cardboard box and a person doing business on a park bench." :-)  An rfcxml "aside" should do the trick.

We need "moar pics!"

### §2

Verification Anchor def: seems to bias towards intra- ("typically")

Layered Attestation def: the fact that the TCB is layered should be an internal detail.

I would add an “Attestation Credential” def to encompass Evidence and Attestation Results.

I believe we would be doing the community a great service if we provided definitive guidance on naming the involved keys.

### §3.1

It says: "the Attesting Environment MUST NOT treat an attestation binder input received from an untrusted host as authoritative without first verifying it has not been substituted."
This seems predicated on the Attesting Environment's ability to continuously monitor the extended TCB state and assess its trustworthiness every time the binder is sent across the TE/AE boundary.
We could remove some of the current vagueness by making the requirements for the AE explicit.

### §3.3

It says: "In the transport context, two deployment variants arise that correspond to the topological timing models defined in Section 5"
The coupling between the arrangement of RATS roles and the timing models seems unwarranted.
It also creates some dissonance with §5.3, "Combining Timing Models".

### §4.4

This one's a tough cookie :-)

It is unclear what "eviction" and "eviction signalling" refer to.  They don't seem to appear anywhere else.

It says" "[...] transport-layer routing obligations" which seems to downplay what a real L7 device can do somewhat.

### §5

Should the title be “Timing Models”? (“Topology" is about space, not time.)

I'd add a reference to the paper by Arto et al. that introduced the pre-/intra-/post- nomenclature: https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1007/978-3-030-91625-1_10

In keeping with the “moar pics” theme, we could show a breakdown of the two timing models to illustrate how the elementary actions are sequenced differently:

* Intra-

```
secure channel session initialisation

binder derivation from session

attestation credential creation using binder

attestation credential delivery

  attestation credential receipt

  attestation credential binder extraction

  attestation credential binder check

  attestation credential verification

  transport session finalisation

secure and attested channel session established
```

* Post-

```
secure transport session established

binder derivation from session

attestation credential creation using binder

attestation credential delivery

  attestation credential receipt

  attestation credential binder extraction

  attestation credential binder check

  attestation credential verification

attested channel session established
```

### §5.2

It says: "Post-handshake is an application-layer mechanism."
It is unclear what "mechanism" is supposed to mean in this context.

### 6

"Root Secret” is not necessarily secret, is it?  The key feature of the binder is unpredictability, not privacy.

### 6.1

This breaks the e2e invariant provided by the secure transport layer, requiring a new way to establish the invariant at a higher layer.
This increases the complexity of implementation and deployment, and therefore, fragility.
Do we really want to go there?

The term "out-of-band" doesn't sound entirely appropriate. I believe the proxy is still assumed to be on-path, no?

comments.author: telephonicrobotics
comments.body:
Thanks for the review! I'm going to jump on the most contentious part and address the others in a separate reply. 

> ### §4.4
> This one's a tough cookie :-)
> 
> It is unclear what "eviction" and "eviction signalling" refer to. They don't seem to appear anywhere else.
> 
> It says" "[...] transport-layer routing obligations" which seems to downplay what a real L7 device can do somewhat.
> 
> <snip>
> ### 6.1
> This breaks the e2e invariant provided by the secure transport layer, requiring a new way to establish the broken e2e invariant at a higher layer. This increases the complexity of implementation and deployment, and therefore fragility.

>  Do we really want to go there?

As it turns out, yes, kinda (I do). I've roped Hannes in on the idea with some enthusiasm (and Ionut has humoured me, and I also invited Tiru in on it not super long ago-- who may or may not agree). It makes use of [EKU ](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-tls-extended-key-update/). However; I will repeat what I shared with Markus at https://github.com/tls-attestation/use-cases-and-properties/pull/48#issuecomment-4687308877 : 

"I have a concept for how to allow an attestation aware proxy to cooperate without requiring nested encryption, but if that was not to pan out for any number of reasons, then the property would basically just affirm that the protocol should abort the connection if intercepted by a malicious intermediary."

However-- these parts of the review make it clear that these sections needs additional abstractions and smoothing over from stuff that was borrowed over from my other draft I mentioned, so I'll prioritize that to minimize distractions on this document.

issues.title: Ionut's feedback imported from PDF
issues.author: telephonicrobotics
issues.body:
These items are still TODO, not yet addressed by PR #10:
(LLM assisted summary)

---

## §2

~~### Layered Attestation def~~
It says: 
> "A common example is a TEE executing within a virtual machine, which is itself executing on a host platform."

Not sure I follow this expression; maybe it's a case of using different terminology. In my view, the VM is the TEE (e.g., a Trusted Domain on Intel TDX platforms). We should refine the wording here to ensure it represents current confidential computing isolation patterns accurately.

> Note: Addressed in https://github.com/telephonicrobotics/seat-architecture/pull/14 (deleted whole section)

---

## §3.2

### Relying Party definition
It says:
> "The Relying Party consumes Attestation Results or Evidence and uses them to make authorization decisions..."

Don't think this is correct as per RATS architecture. A Relying Party strictly consumes Attestation Results to make downstream authorization decisions. If it evaluates raw Evidence directly, it is functionally fulfilling the role of a Verifier (which matches our co-located topology, but the definitions should remain separated at the role level).

---

## §3.3

### Verifier definition
It says:
> "The Verifier appraises Evidence by applying an Appraisal Policy for Evidence and produces Attestation Results."

You can probably mirror the standard Verifier terminology here and state that it applies an *Appraisal Policy for Evidence* to generate those results, or clarify how the policy objects are structurally designated in the mapping.

### Remote Verifier def
It says:
> "The Attester contacts the Verifier prior to or during the session and obtains Attestation Results, which it then presents to the Relying Party. This variant may be more common in post-handshake attestation flows. This deployment corresponds to the Passport Model of RFC9334."

I don't think Remote Verifiers should be strictly relegated to the Passport model here. A Remote Verifier can easily operate under a Background-Check model where the Relying Party passes the data out-of-band during an active handshake. We should decouple the physical location of the service from the RATS conveyance model choice.

---

## §6

### Attestation Session Binding
Throughout this section, the text explicitly mandates binding the transport session tracking to the "Evidence" payload. 

Note that focusing exclusively on Evidence excludes the Passport model, where the Attester presents pre-obtained Attestation Results to the Relying Party instead of raw Evidence. Broadening our terminology to "Attestation Credentials" or something along those lines throughout this sequence would provide much better architectural agnosticism.

For the sake of comparison, this is the structural topology that I've run `expat` and `early-attestation` drafts against to prove single key compromise resilience. issues.title: Markus' Review
issues.author: telephonicrobotics
issues.body:
_Originally posted by @burgerdev [on the mailing list](https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/seat/cDQRqCD63EAyR-m59W6W3bUO3F0/)_

> Sec 2.
> (tbK): An asymmetric key pair whose private key is generated and maintained exclusively within the Target Environment (e.g., a TEE).
> [...]
> Evidence produced by the Attesting Environment MUST include a binding to the tbK.
> 
> 

- [ ] "This reads to me as if a tbk was mandatory for all attested TLS schemes. However, I don't think a tbk is always necessary and I'd thus like to avoid setting that requirement in stone. Sufficient for me would be to condition the requirement, along the lines of "if a tbk is used, it needs to be bound ...". Same concern for the "Key Non-exportability" paragraph in section 10."

Comments: A similar question was also raised in an issue by Markus [here ](https://github.com/tls-attestation/exported-attestation/issues/58)

Markus followed-up with a concrete use-case to consider which I've added via a PR here: https://github.com/tls-attestation/use-cases-and-properties/pull/56


> Sec 6.1
> [RFC9334] expects a failed Attester appraisal to result in reduced access or privileges rather than outright rejection.
> In the event of failures occurring within the Post-Handshake Window, this behaviour is to be handled at the transport layer.
> 
> 

- [ ] "This seems to be at odds with the definition of the post-handshake window in sec. 2, which explicitly allows the application layer to handle attestation, and with the guidance in the following paragraph. Is this a load-bearing requirement, or can it just be relaxed?"


> 9.3. Attestation Key Correlation
> 
> 

- [ ] "This seems to be a general consideration for RATS, if there is no conclusion for attested TLS I'd just remove it."


> Sec 10
> When a transport session is resumed, previously obtained Attestation Credential may no longer reflect the Attester's current state. Attestation from a prior session does not carry over to a resumed session.
> 
> 

- [ ] "This seems to be overly restrictive: even if I accept the need for periodic re-attestation (which I don't), I don't see why resumption needs to be outright forbidden. Either describe a concern which applies universally, or relax the requirement?"

pulls.title: Initial patch based on various co-author feedback
pulls.author: telephonicrobotics
pulls.body:
Addresses an initial batch of unresolved feedback compiled across two separate reviews: Thomas Fossati's issue review (Issue #6) and Ionut Mihalcea's inline PDF annotations.

This represents a partial resolution of the open commentary. Outstanding structural and architectural items will be tracked via dedicated follow-up work items.

---

* **Change**: Added reference `NIEME2021` ("Trusted Sockets Layer: A TLS 1.3 Based Trusted Channel Protocol"). (Thomas)

* **Change**: Added Gene Spafford's quote regarding cryptography and system integrity as an `rfcxml` aside block. (Thomas)

* **Change**: Explicitly stated that "transport" and "secure transport" are used interchangeably throughout the architecture document. (Thomas)

* **Change**: Formally acknowledged the adoption of terms coined by `NIEME2021`. (Thomas)

* **Change**: Updated the definition of `Attestation Timing Model` to reference "connection establishment time" instead of "transport handshake completion". (Ionut)

* **Change**: Rephrased `Evidence Generation Time` to state that evidence reflects the reported state when underlying Claims were collected, rather than an absolute snapshot of the exact millisecond of signing. (Ionut)

comments.body:
This is a bit confusing. The Attester always presents an Attestation Credential to the RP. The RP might sometimes need to send that credential to a Verifier to get a different one back (this is based on the current definition above). Might be better to change the definition of Attestation Credential to "whatever the Attester sends to the RP, regardless of whether it's Evidence or AR". So it's not necessarily a term for "one of {Evidence, AR}", just syntactic sugar for what's passed between those specific participants.

(it's late, the above paragraph might not make much sense, feedback is welcome :D )

So what do we think about binding ARs to the connection, in the end? I think this point has flopped both ways. Binding means better security. Not binding means better perf. For use-cases where perf is critical it doesn't sound far-fetched that unbound ARs would be preferred. I guess it comes down to what your acceptable threat model looks like.

@ionut-arm 
> So what do we think about binding ARs to the connection, in the end? I think this point has flopped both ways. Binding means better security. Not binding means better perf. 

> For use-cases where perf is critical it doesn't sound far-fetched that unbound ARs would be preferred. I guess it comes down to what your acceptable threat model looks like.

Hrm. Is https://github.com/telephonicrobotics/seat-architecture/blob/main/img/arch.ascii-art  another example of background-check only? :D To be honest, the formal analysis is always assuming that the Client is a so-called "Verifying Relying Party". So, I would say I am a bit less confident about how AR binding works at like the concrete API/wire format level. 

edit: Let me try and unpack that.

The formal models deeply compress a lot:

1. RP Client connects to Attesting Server
2. Attesting Server collects claims, generates Evidence, gets it signed by "AK"
3. Evidence is conveyed back to the RP Client by the Attesting Server in a CMW
4. RP Client appraises the Evidence and compares the nonce with what’s expected, checks if they trust AK, the TLS identity signing key etc

The end. 

There's obviously more going on in the real world, yeah? But that’s background check. 

If an RP is being served an AR from 12 minutes ago, that nonce isn’t getting attested, right? Or does it depend on how complex a team wants to build out an RFC9334 aligned system in the real world?
I honestly think this one is just trying to deal with the fact that I feel 'Attestation Credential' is overloaded here and was uncertain about how to unpack it.
Ooh, I see the challenge is an open issue, at least in the editors copy of ‘early’ it seems https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-fossati-seat-early-attestation-04.html#name-verification

When discussing passport, we tend to conflate the freshness model and the topological pattern, but these are actually orthogonal.

In our case, an AR could be generated when the transport connection is established and used once, or it could be created before the transport connection begins and used one or more times.

I believe the former (“fresh, single use passport”) should be fully compatible with the background check and verifying-relying party simplification made in current models because the freshness/binding properties are essentially the same.

The second use (“reusable passport”) has not yet been modelled in the aTLS context, at least as far as I am aware.  So, its security is a big question mark.

@thomas-fossati thanks. I see expat say little that is super helpful; https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-fossati-seat-expat-02.html#name-architecture

Okay. Well, on one hand, again I am glad I am not crazy, but on the other hand I see that part of why I struggled with this is because this hasn’t been modeled! I wonder what choices where made over with LAKE RA…

@thomas-fossati @ionut-arm

https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-lake-ra-05.html#name-instantiation-of-remote-att

LAKE RA chose both options for
Passport.  Option A is cached and I suppose the security properties are reduced to that of the EDHOC’s typical assumptions. And then option B looks like a 3 party loop? 

 I propose we borrow LAKE’s homework

> I wonder what choices where made over with LAKE RA…

The RA document appears to support both modes (see the [third para of §5.4](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-lake-ra-05.html#section-5.4-3)).

Probably worth asking Yuxuan (ysong02 on G-H) whether this choice is backed by formal analysis.

Apologies, I didn’t refresh the page and therefore didn’t see your comment!

In any case, before borrowing the cached AR option from LAKE, I suggest we establish whether any formal proof is available.  If not, it should be explicitly noted.

(Also, a random thought: if we allow cached AR, we probably need to evaluate its impact — if any — on re-attestation.)
Alternatively, the RP can compute the binder locally and send it to the verifier which compares it with the binder in the Evidence. It has an advantage that RP does not have to decode the Evidence.

The charter text says:

A Standards Track document defining an attested (D)TLS protocol extension supporting remote peer and mutual attestation bound to the (D)TLS connection.

It needs to be discussed in the WG whether the optimization to not bind the AR to the TLS session is acceptable or not.

> It needs to be discussed in the WG whether the optimization to not bind the AR to the TLS session is acceptable or not.

Alternatively, the discussion could be about how strict the threat model can be given various forms of binding. For example, I'd consider an AR that contains a claim about an attested key to be bound to the connection if that key signs the handshake, but it offers a lower security bar.

> […] I'd consider an AR that contains a claim about an attested key to be bound to the connection if that key signs the handshake, but it offers a lower security bar.

The presence of the TLS key is a basic requirement for any AR that wants to be used in TLS.  This should be stated prominently.

On top of that, the debate should focus on acceptable levels of freshness and session binding for ARs.

I don't know if y'all have read it already, but [draft-zhang-seat-selection](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-zhang-seat-selection/) has kicked off a (fairly high-level) assessment of different integration models, though they don't cover these options AFAICT, and the modelling doesn't go that deep.

> I don't know if y'all have read it already, but [draft-zhang-seat-selection](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-zhang-seat-selection/) has kicked off a (fairly high-level) assessment of different integration models, though they don't cover these options AFAICT, and the modelling doesn't go that deep.

Yes, I read it; they make good observations.

I don't agree intra-handshake is impacted by firewalls; TLS 1.3 requires firewall to act as proxy. If a firewall is just inspecting TLS traffic, it does not have any visibility into a the handshake beyond ClientHello and ServerHello. Further, with Encrypted ClientHello, the visibility further reduces.

> I don't agree intra-handshake is impacted by firewalls; TLS 1.3 requires firewall to act as proxy. If a firewall is just inspecting TLS traffic, it does not have any visibility into a the handshake beyond ClientHello and ServerHello. Further, with Encrypted ClientHello, the visibility further reduces.

Sure, not all their observations are necessarily correct. That doesn’t detract, though, from the fact that their observations are interesting and worthy of discussion.

@tireddy2 @thomas-fossati @ionut-arm 
> The charter text says:
>
>> A Standards Track document defining an attested (D)TLS protocol extension supporting remote peer and mutual attestation bound to the (D)TLS connection.
>

I agree that the WG should be asked, although I think that the following also from the charter gives us some leeway:

> The attested (D)TLS protocol extension will **allow** per-connection [freshness](https://www.ietf.org/rfc/rfc9334.html#section-10) of Evidence and Attestation Results.

In my view that means that we will need to emulate the 3-party round-trip like LAKE RA uses with the passport model, but at the very same time, by *allowing* per-connection freshness of Attestation Results in that way, I believe we would be in the position to offer a cached version, as the charter doesn't state per-freshness as strictly **mandatory** as long as per-freshness for AR is *possible*.
